dim_1_core_thesis.premise: Nobody and nothing outside yourself can ruin your emotional equilibrium unless you surrender your emotional autonomy; external events merely act as triggers that expose your pre-existing, unhealed internal insecurities and the negative stories your mind invents.
dim_1_core_thesis.paradigm_shift: Conventional intuition blames external circumstances and other people for our emotional pain ('He ruined my mood', 'They made me angry'). The radical paradigm shift reveals that external events are neutral facts; emotional suffering is entirely self-manufactured when we project our internal unworthiness into catastrophic narratives and hand the remote control of our nervous system to external actors.

dim_2_causal_model.mechanism: The Causal Cascade of Emotional Reactivity: External Neutral Event (Unanswered text, unappreciated effort, social exclusion) -> Narrative Meaning Assignment ('They choose others over me; I am unworthy') -> Amplified Emotional Intensity (Surrendering the emotional remote control) -> Outward Projection & Grievance ('Why did they do this to me?') -> Reinforcement of Unresolved Shadow Patterns. Inversion Protocol: Inward Inquiry Shift ('Why did I react this way?') -> Diagnostic Identification of Past Wounds -> Reclaiming Emotional Sovereignty.
dim_2_causal_model.ratios_in_prose: The causal model demonstrates that the raw external stimulus represents less than 10% of emotional variance, while 90%+ of affective intensity is generated by the internal narrative assigned to the stimulus. Replacing a single outward-blaming question with an inward diagnostic inquiry yields an immediate pivot from emotional victimhood to self-mastery.

dim_3_master_analogy.analogy: The Emotional Remote Control & The Film Projector: Handing someone else the remote control to your television allows them to flip channels and blast jarring noise at will. Similarly, your mind operates as a film projector that beams your past unhealed rejection reels onto the blank white screen of neutral external events—mistaking the projection for the reality of the screen.

classifications.symptom: Experiencing an immediate collapse of mood or day over a single neutral slight, unreplied text, or social exclusion.
classifications.etiology: Assigning an internal catastrophic meaning ('They always choose others, I am not good enough') rather than recognizing the plain external fact.

classifications.symptom: Intense anger, defensive hostility, or deep shame when excluded or unappreciated.
classifications.etiology: Past unintegrated experiences of feeling ignored, abandoned, or conditionally valued only when achieving external approval.

classifications.symptom: Believing that one's happiness or peace is held hostage by the words, tones, and gestures of peers or superiors.
classifications.etiology: Lack of internal differentiation between affect generation and external reality.

failure_modes: Suppression Fallacy: Attempting to become stoic by asserting 'I must not feel anything', which represses emotions instead of observing them without losing self-control.
Outward Grievance Spiral: Fixating on 'Why did this person do this to me?' which validates helplessness and locks the individual in perpetual victimhood.
Equating Neutral Facts with Personal Worth: Confusing an absent invitation or slow text reply with definitive proof of personal inadequacy.

algorithm: 1. Notice the Mood Drop: The instant your mood collapses over someone's action or silence, halt immediately and label the somatic activation.
2. Separate Fact from Story: Isolate the objective fact (e.g., 'They didn't invite me to the gathering') from the manufactured narrative (e.g., 'Nobody values me, I am unwanted').

3. Execute the Inward Attribution Shift: Immediately replace the instinctive question 'Why did they do this to me?' with 'Why did I react this way? What past insecurity or rejection wound does this touch?'
4. Practice Non-Loss of Self: Allow the physical emotion to exist without acting on it impulsively, affirming: 'I can feel this emotion, but I refuse to lose myself to it.'

dim_6_skeptic_box.pop_culture_distortion: Pop culture and internet memes often misrepresent emotional resilience as cold detachment, apathy, or toxic positivity ('Never let anyone see you sweat', 'Don't care about anything').
dim_6_skeptic_box.clinical_empirical_reality: In clinical depth psychology and cognitive neuroscience, true emotional resilience does not mean numbness or dissociation. Humans naturally experience immediate affective responses; resilience lies in metacognitive appraisal—the capacity to decouple the raw somatic reaction from self-loathing narratives and conscious behavioral choices.

proposed_concepts.name: Jungian Trigger Diagnostic
proposed_concepts.definition: The psychodynamic diagnostic principle (rooted in Carl Jung's shadow psychology) asserting that an acute emotional reaction to an external provocation is not caused by the external event itself, but functions as an unconscious diagnostic signal pointing directly to an individual's unhealed internal insecurities, rejection trauma, and latent behavioral patterns.

proposed_concepts.name: Cognitive Appraisal Separation
proposed_concepts.definition: The psychological distinction between an objective external reality and the internal cognitive meaning assigned to it. When an individual unconsciously projects their internal insecurity onto a neutral or ambiguous event, the resulting negative narrative intensifies distress, effectively surrendering emotional control to external actors.

proposed_concepts.name: Inward Attribution Shift
proposed_concepts.definition: The cognitive reframing intervention that deliberately converts outward victimized accusation ('Why did they do this to me?') into inward analytical curiosity ('Why did I react this way?'). This shift breaks emotional contagion, restores agency, and permits the experiencing of affect without emotional dysregulation or loss of self.

proposed_relationships.description: Unresolved self-directed loathing reinforces cognitive vulnerability to external triggers.

recall_cards.question: What does Carl Jung identify as the true source when someone or something triggers you?
recall_cards.answer: According to Carl Jung, whatever triggers you points directly to your own unresolved insecurities, past wounds, or unexamined shadow patterns—not the external event itself.

recall_cards.question: What is the core cognitive mechanism that intensifies an emotional reaction to a neutral situation (such as not being invited to a party)?
recall_cards.answer: The internal story and catastrophic meaning assigned to the situation (e.g., 'They always pick others; I am unworthy') intensifies the emotional distress far beyond the objective fact itself.

recall_cards.question: What single question shift transforms emotional reactivity into psychological sovereignty?
recall_cards.answer: Shifting from the victimized inquiry 'Why did this person do this to me?' to the diagnostic self-inquiry 'Why did I react this way?'.
